title: Edmond v. United States (1997)
summary: An inferior officer is one whose work is directed and supervised at some level by others who were appointed by the President with Senate consent, so civilian judges of the Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals may be appointed by the Secretary of Transportation.
notes:
Key line: Whether one is an inferior officer depends on whether he has a superior. (Justice Scalia)

Citation: 520 U.S. 651 (1997).

sections.Parties: The petitioners were Jon Edmond and five other members of the Coast Guard, Lazenby, Leaver, Leonard, Nichols and Venable, each convicted by court-martial. The respondent was the United States. The officials whose status was disputed were the two civilian judges of the Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals, Chief Judge Joseph H. Baum and Associate Judge Alfred F. Bridgman, Jr. Alan B. Morrison argued for petitioners, and Malcolm L. Stewart argued for the United States. The case concerned who could appoint the civilian judges and whether they were principal officers needing Senate confirmation.
sections.Material Facts: The Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals, formerly the Coast Guard Court of Military Review, hears appeals from courts-martial; its decisions are reviewable by the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces. Under Article 66(a) of the Uniform Code of Military Justice its judges may be commissioned officers or civilians. Judges Baum and Bridgman were originally assigned to the court by the General Counsel of the Department of Transportation, who is ex officio Judge Advocate General of the Coast Guard. After doubts arose, the Secretary of Transportation issued a memorandum adopting the General Counsel's assignments as appointments of his own under 49 U.S.C. section 323(a), which lets the Secretary appoint and fix the pay of officers and employees of the Department. Petitioners' six convictions were affirmed by panels including one or both civilian judges after the Secretary acted.
sections.Procedural History: Courts-martial convicted each petitioner. The Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals or its predecessor affirmed with one or both civilian judges participating after the Secretary's appointment memorandum. The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces affirmed the convictions, 45 M.J. 19, 44 M.J. 278 and 44 M.J. 272, relying on its holding on remand in Ryder that the Secretary's appointments were valid and cured the earlier defect. The Supreme Court granted certiorari in No. 96-262 and the five companion cases, heard argument on February 24, 1997, and decided the case on May 19, 1997, affirming. Justice Scalia wrote for the Court, with eight Justices joining in full and Justice Souter joining Parts I and II.
sections.Issue: First, did Congress authorize the Secretary of Transportation to appoint civilian judges of the Coast Guard Court of Criminal Appeals, given that section 323(a) speaks generally of officers and employees of the Department while Article 66(a) of the Code refers to judges assigned by the Judge Advocate General? Second, if the Secretary had statutory authority, is his appointment of these judges constitutional under the Appointments Clause, which permits Congress to vest the appointment of inferior officers in Heads of Departments but requires principal officers to be nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate? The answer turned on how to distinguish principal from inferior officers.
sections.Holding: Congress authorized the appointments. Section 323(a) by its plain terms covers officers of the Department, including judges of the Coast Guard court, and Article 66(a) concerns assignment rather than appointment; reading it to let the Judge Advocate General appoint would make it unconstitutional, because the Clause does not allow such an officer to appoint even inferior officers. The appointments are constitutional because the judges are inferior officers. Their work is directed and supervised by the Judge Advocate General, who prescribes rules of procedure and may remove them from judicial assignment without cause, and by the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, which reviews their decisions. They cannot render a final decision for the United States unless other executive officers permit it. Judgments affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Scalia first resolved the statutory question by ordinary reading. Section 323(a) is a general grant to appoint officers of the Department; nothing excludes judges, and Weiss v. United States had already treated assignment and appointment as different acts under the Code. He then turned to the constitutional line. The Court had never set a definitive test, and Morrison v. Olson had relied on factors such as limited duties and tenure without saying they were necessary. The term inferior officer, Scalia reasoned, implies a relationship to a superior below the President, not merely lesser importance. In the context of a Clause designed to preserve political accountability, inferior officers are those whose work is directed and supervised at some level by officers who were themselves appointed with Senate confirmation. The First Congress's 1789 statutes creating departments with subordinate chief clerks confirmed this reading. Here the Judge Advocate General exercises administrative oversight, may prescribe rules and can remove a judge from the court without cause, a powerful tool of control. The Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces reviews every decision, though under a standard that defers on factual sufficiency. The decisive point was that these judges have no power to render a final decision on behalf of the United States unless permitted by other executive officers. Freytag, which held special trial judges to be inferior officers, did not hold that Tax Court judges are principal officers, so it did not conflict.

topics.lrs-s-inferior-officer: Combined administrative and adjudicative supervision supported inferior status despite substantial jurisdiction.

learning.separateOpinions: Nine to zero on the judgment. Justice Souter concurred in part and in the judgment. He agreed that supervision by higher officers is a necessary condition for inferior status but thought it not sufficient; he would also weigh the significance of the officer's duties, and on that fuller inquiry he agreed that these judges are inferior officers.
